say.en: "It is raining" is either true or false. "Close the door!" is neither. Logic starts by sorting sentences like these, then joins them with and, or, not, if...then. In this lesson: Identify propositions and their truth values.
Use the connectives ¬, ∧, ∨, gives and ↔.
Build truth tables for compound propositions.

body.en: A proposition is a declarative statement that is either true (1) or false (0), but not both. *Propositions* are joined by connectives to form compound propositions (well-formed formulae): negation ¬p (not p), conjunction p ∧ q (p and q), disjunction p ∨ q (p or q, inclusive), conditional p → q (if p then q) and biconditional p ↔ q (p if and only if q). Questions, commands and exclamations are not propositions.

points.en: ¬p is true when p is false
p ∧ q true only when both are true
p ∨ q false only when both are false
p → q false only when p is true and q false
p ↔ q true when p and q are equal

title.en: Truth tables and the converse family

body.en: A *truth* table lists the value of a formula for every combination of its variables: n variables need 2^n rows. For the conditional p → q, three related statements are named: the converse q → p, the inverse ¬p → ¬q and the contrapositive ¬q → ¬p. The contrapositive is always equivalent to the original statement; the converse and the inverse are equivalent to each other but not to the original.

say.en: A truth table lists the value of a formula for every combination of its variables: n variables need 2^n rows. For the conditional p gives q, three related statements are named: the converse q gives p, the inverse ¬p gives ¬q and the contrapositive ¬q gives ¬p. The contrapositive is always equivalent to the original statement; the converse and the inverse are equivalent to each other but not to the original. n variables gives 2^n rows.
Converse: q gives p.
Inverse: ¬p gives ¬q.
Contrapositive: ¬q gives ¬p (is equivalent to p gives q).
